The dielectric scattering problem is modeled by Maxwell's equations with transmission conditions on the interface and the Silver-Müller radiation condition at infinity.
Standard boundary integral formulations involve two coupled equations for electric and magnetic currents on the interface.
The Kleinman-Martin method reduces the problem to a single integral equation for a single unknown density on the interface.
Four different families of integral equations are derived, parameterized by two complex parameters a and b.
Choosing parameters appropriately eliminates spurious interior resonances and ensures unique solvability for all real frequencies.
The operator C* is a self-adjoint, elliptic boundary integral operator used as a regularizer.
The integral operators are Fredholm of index zero in the space H^{-1/2}(div_Γ, Γ) of tangential vector fields.
The associated interior boundary value problem involves a boundary condition aγ_D u - b C* γ_N u = 0.
Uniqueness of the dielectric scattering problem solution holds if the exterior wave number κ_e is real positive or has positive imaginary part.
The Helmholtz decomposition represents tangential vector fields as pairs of scalar fields, simplifying operator analysis.
The paper proves well-posedness of the integral equations on both smooth and Lipschitz continuous boundaries.
The Silver-Müller radiation condition ensures the scattered field behaves like an outgoing wave at infinity.
The single-layer potential and double-layer potential operators are fundamental in constructing the integral equations.
The Calderón projectors P and P_c satisfy P ◦ P_c = 0 and relate the boundary integral operators C and M.
The paper provides explicit integral representations for the interior and exterior fields in terms of the unknown density j.
The integral equations derived are of the second kind and contain compact perturbations of identity operators.
The method generalizes the Kleinman-Martin approach from scalar acoustic problems to vector electromagnetic problems.
The paper uses variational methods and energy space techniques to analyze the integral equations.
The approach is motivated by computational advantages of single integral equations over coupled systems.
The paper includes a proof of uniqueness for the dielectric scattering problem under stated assumptions.
